The electrification of energy systems is also occurring in tandem with infrastructure digitalization, creating vulnerabilities from cyberattacks and electromagnetic pulses. The electrification and digitization of the grid also intensify existing risks tied to the reliance on Global Positioning System (GPS) for precise time synchronization for grid management. These unencrypted, publicly accessible civil signals are susceptible to jamming and spoofing. Without proper mitigation, these threats have the potential to render large portions of interconnected energy infrastructure inoperable, leaving DOW equipment and installations reliant solely on backup power not dependent on electrified infrastructure and potentially creating significant resupply and operational continuity challenges. Moreover, damage to local transmission infrastructure (e.g., weather-induced or human-caused) carries higher consequences with electrification and can disrupt power deliveries to U.S. forces regardless of mutual use or local agreements regarding priority service. For example, winter storm Uri knocked out power across the southern United States in 2021, leaving some military installations without power for several days and others realizing how poorly prepared they were to secure enough diesel fuel to keep backup generators running (U.S. Congress 2022). Outside of the continental United States, reliance on external power grids can cause more acute vulnerabilities, as local grids in host nations might not be configured to handle the increased load associated with a surge in U.S. troop presence. Such demand-side considerations for DOW are already present in non-conflict conditions, including in Guam. The U.S. Navy, which accounts for approximately 20% of Guam’s utility power sales, voluntarily switches to standby generators during periods of peak demand to help prevent power outages (Scarpitti and Voss 2024; Pacific Daily News 2024). While such challenges can often be managed during peacetime through coordination and advanced planning, the situation could be more precarious in a contested environment, when adversaries may target local energy infrastructure, logistical routes may be disrupted, and host- nation priorities may shift, all of which can magnify the operational risks associated with electrification. Additionally, the increased digitization of energy systems is lowering the barrier for adversaries to operate in operational technology (OT) environments that were once the domain of specialized engineers, a trend compounded by the use of AI-driven adversarial techniques that further reduce the expertise required to disrupt military energy systems. With many warfighting missions originating from within the continental United States, U.S. domestic power grid reliability is directly linked to the ability to project power. Infrastructure component shortages, increasing load demand, and inadequate transmission infrastructure might pose a risk to the U.S. power grid’s ability to support national security objectives.
